{{Short description|Measure with complex values}}

In [[mathematics]], specifically [[measure theory]], a '''complex measure''' generalizes the concept of [[measure (mathematics)|measure]] by letting it have [[complex number|complex]] values.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Tao |first=Terence |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HoGDAwAAQBAJ&dq=complex+measure+measure+theory&pg=PP1 |title=An Introduction to Measure Theory |date=2011-09-14 |publisher=American Mathematical Soc. |isbn=978-0-8218-6919-2 |language=en}}</ref> In other words, one allows for [[Set (mathematics)|sets]] whose size (length, area, volume) is a [[complex number]].

== Definition ==

Formally, a ''complex measure'' <math> \mu </math> on a [[sigma-algebra|measurable space]] <math> (X,\Sigma) </math> is a complex-valued [[function (mathematics)|function]]

:<math>\mu: \Sigma \to \mathbb{C}</math>

that is [[sigma additivity|sigma-additive]]. In other words, for any [[sequence]] <math>(A_{n})_{n \in \mathbb{N}}</math> of [[disjoint sets]] belonging to <math> \Sigma </math>, one has

:<math>\sum_{n = 1}^{\infty} \mu(A_{n}) = \mu \left( \bigcup_{n = 1}^{\infty} A_{n} \right) \in \mathbb{C}.</math>

As <math>\displaystyle \bigcup_{n = 1}^{\infty} A_{n} = \bigcup_{n = 1}^{\infty} A_{\sigma(n)}</math> for any [[permutation]] ([[bijection]]) <math> \sigma: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} </math>, it follows that <math>\displaystyle \sum_{n = 1}^{\infty} \mu(A_{n})</math> [[Unconditional convergence|converges unconditionally]] (hence, since <math>\mathbb{C}</math> is finite dimensional, <math>\mu</math> [[Absolute convergence|converges absolutely]]).

== Integration with respect to a complex measure ==

One can define the ''integral'' of a complex-valued [[measurable function]] with respect to a complex measure in the same way as the [[Lebesgue integral]] of a [[Real number|real]]-valued measurable function with respect to a [[Measure (mathematics)|non-negative measure]], by approximating a measurable function with [[simple function]]s.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Tao |first=Terence |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HoGDAwAAQBAJ&dq=complex+measure+measure+theory&pg=PP1 |title=An Introduction to Measure Theory |date=2011-09-14 |publisher=American Mathematical Soc. |isbn=978-0-8218-6919-2 |language=en}}</ref> Just as in the case of ordinary integration, this more general integral might fail to exist, or its value might be infinite (the [[Riemann sphere|complex infinity]]).

Another approach is to not develop a theory of integration from scratch, but rather use the already available concept of integral of a [[real-valued function]] with respect to a non-negative measure.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Taylor |first=Michael Eugene |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=AwUPCgAAQBAJ&dq=complex+measure+measure+theory&pg=PP1 |title=Measure Theory and Integration |date=2006 |publisher=American Mathematical Soc. |isbn=978-0-8218-4180-8 |language=en}}</ref> To that end, it is a quick check that the real and imaginary parts &mu;<sub>1</sub> and &mu;<sub>2</sub> of a complex measure &mu; are finite-valued [[signed measure]]s. One can apply the [[Hahn decomposition theorem|Hahn-Jordan decomposition]] to these measures to split them as

:<math>\mu_1=\mu_1^+-\mu_1^-</math>

and

:<math>\mu_2=\mu_2^+-\mu_2^-</math>

where &mu;<sub>1</sub><sup>+</sup>, &mu;<sub>1</sub><sup>−</sup>, &mu;<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>, &mu;<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> are finite-valued non-negative measures (which are unique in some sense). Then, for a measurable function ''f'' which is ''real-valued'' for the moment, one can define

:<math>\int_X \! f \, d\mu = \left(\int_X \! f \, d\mu_1^+ - \int_X \! f \, d\mu_1^-\right) + i \left(\int_X \! f \, d\mu_2^+ - \int_X \! f \, d\mu_2^-\right) </math>

as long as the expression on the right-hand side is defined, that is, all four integrals exist and when adding them up one does not encounter the [[indeterminate form|indeterminate]] &infin;&minus;&infin;.<ref name=":0" />

Given now a ''complex-valued'' measurable function, one can integrate its real and imaginary components separately as illustrated above and define, as expected,

:<math>\int_X \! f \, d\mu = \int_X \! \Re(f) \, d\mu + i \int_X \! \Im(f) \, d\mu.</math>

== Variation of a complex measure and polar decomposition ==

For a complex measure &mu;, one defines its ''variation'', or ''[[absolute value]]'', |&mu;| by the formula

:<math>|\mu|(A)= \sup\sum_{n=1}^\infty |\mu(A_n)|</math>

where ''A'' is in &Sigma; and the [[supremum]] runs over all sequences of [[disjoint sets]] (''A''<sub>''n''</sub>)<sub>''n''</sub> whose [[Union (set theory)|union]] is ''A''. Taking only finite partitions of the set ''A'' into [[Measurable set|measurable subsets]], one obtains an equivalent definition.

It turns out that |&mu;| is a non-negative finite measure. In the same way as a complex number can be represented in  a [[complex number|polar form]], one has a ''polar decomposition'' for a complex measure: There exists a measurable function &theta; with real values such that

:<math>d\mu = e ^{i \theta}d |\mu|,</math>

meaning

:<math>\int_X f\, d\mu = \int_X  f e ^{i \theta} \, d |\mu|</math>

for any [[absolutely integrable]] measurable function ''f'', i.e., ''f'' satisfying

:<math>\int_X |f|\, d|\mu|<\infty.</math>

One can use the [[Radon–Nikodym theorem]] to prove that the variation is a measure and the existence of the [[polar decomposition]].

== The space of complex measures==

The sum of two complex measures is a complex measure, as is the product of a complex measure by a complex number. That is to say, the set of all complex measures on a measure space (''X'', &Sigma;) forms a [[vector space]] over the complex numbers. Moreover, the ''[[total variation]]'' <math>\|\cdot\|</math> defined as

:<math>\|\mu\| = |\mu| (X)\, </math>

is a [[Norm (mathematics)|norm]], with respect to which the space of complex measures is a [[Banach space]].
